facts: Mendoza makes nearly two-thirds of Argentina's wine, with vineyards in the eastern foothills of the Andes at an average of 2,000 to 3,600 feet above sea level.
Luján de Cuyo became Argentina's first delineated appellation in 1993, and it is known particularly for Malbec grown at 2,600 to 3,600 feet.
The climate is continental and semi-arid desert, and the main worry is summer hail, known locally as La Piedra.
Soils are mostly alluvial, loose sand over clay, and vines depend on Andes glacier melt, irrigation channels and boreholes for water.
The Uco Valley is a notable sub-region of Mendoza, which produces more than 60% of Argentine wine.
Argentina's most highly rated Malbec comes from the high-altitude districts of Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley, in Andes foothills between 2,800 and 5,000 feet.
In the high-altitude vineyards of Tupungato, in the Uco Valley, Chardonnay is increasing in popularity.
High altitude and low humidity mean Argentine vineyards rarely face insects, fungi or mold, so growers can use little or no pesticide.
Barossa Shiraz, often from old vines, is a full-bodied red with rich chocolate and spice notes, and some Shiraz vineyards have vines 100 to 150 years old.
Rieslings labelled simply Barossa often include more fruit from the cooler Eden Valley, because the Barossa zone geographical indication also covers Eden Valley.
Clare Valley is one of Australia's oldest wine regions and is best known for Riesling, which it regards as its Australian home.
It lies in the Mid North of South Australia, about 88 miles north of Adelaide, and was registered as an Australian Geographical Indication on 25 March 1999.
Vines grow at 1,300 to 1,600 feet, and the altitude keeps nights cool even in summer, so fruit ripens more evenly and slowly.
Rain falls mostly in winter and spring, averaging around 25 inches a year, and dry summers keep fungal disease to a minimum.
The region has no legally defined subregions, but it is informally split into Auburn, Clare, Polish Hill River, Sevenhill and Watervale.
Coonawarra, in the Limestone Coast zone of South Australia, is known for Cabernet Sauvignon grown on its terra rossa soil.
The terra rossa strip covers just about 9 by 1.2 miles north of Penola and sits on a shallow limestone ridge above swampy land.
West of the ridge the black rendzina soil is poorly drained and much less favorable, while a transitional brown rendzina grows vines quite successfully.
The climate is somewhat maritime, similar to Bordeaux, with 9 inches of rain in the growing season (October to April) out of 23 inches a year.
Extensive cloud cover keeps January temperatures down to about 66°F.
Shiraz was the most widely planted grape in the early days, and the limestone also suits Chardonnay, Riesling and Sauvignon blanc.
The Hunter Valley zone covers the whole Hunter River catchment, and the Hunter region has three named subregions: Upper Hunter Valley, Broke Fordwich and Pokolbin.
The climate is humid subtropical with Pacific influence, making it one of Australia's hottest and wettest wine regions, with more than two thirds of rain falling from October to April.
Rain at harvest is the chief viticultural hazard, so growers choose well-drained sites and keep canopies open to fight bunch rot.
Hunter Semillon is usually unoaked, austere with lemon and grass notes when young, and after 10 plus years in bottle it turns rich and mineral with biscuit notes.
The Upper Hunter is drier and hotter than the Lower Hunter, with 24 inches of annual rain against 28 inches, and irrigation is needed for many vineyards.
Margaret River is in southwest Western Australia, with 14,430 acres under vine and 215 wineries as of 2012.
Its climate is more strongly maritime than any other major Australian region, with a mean annual temperature range of only 13.7°F.
Rainfall is strongly Mediterranean, with only 8 of the annual 46 inches falling between October and April, and overall the climate resembles Bordeaux in a dry vintage.
The main grapes are Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Sauvignon blanc, Sémillon, Shiraz, Merlot and Chenin Blanc.
The region makes just two percent of Australian wine grape production but over 20 percent of the premium wine market.
There are no official subregions, but in 1999 John Gladstones suggested six: Yallingup, Carbunup, Wilyabrup, Treeton, Wallcliffe and Karridale.
Yarra Valley is a cool climate region east of Melbourne, best known for Chardonnay, sparkling wine and Pinot Noir.
The Valley Floor sits mostly at 160 to 260 feet, is warmer on average, and has mainly grey soils with pockets of granite and limestone.
The Upper Yarra rises to about 1,300 feet with younger, fertile red soils and a cooler climate, producing the area's most notable Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
The Yarra Valley was Victoria's first planted wine region, beginning with Yering Station in 1838, but by 1937 it was entirely converted to dairy farming.
Cooler regions like the Yarra Valley lead a move to leaner, acid-driven Chardonnay, with less malolactic conversion and less new oak.
Austrian wines are mostly dry whites, with Grüner Veltliner the dominant white grape, and about 30% of wines are red, made from Blaufränkisch, Pinot noir and Zweigelt.
Districtus Austriae Controllatus (DAC) is the Austrian appellation system, similar to the French AOC, and regional wine committees award it to wines typical of their region.
There are now 18 DACs, starting with Weinviertel DAC from vintage 2002 and including Wachau DAC from vintage 2020.
Zweigelt and Blauburger, both bred at Klosterneuburg in the 1920s, account for nearly half of Austria's red wine.
Mittelburgenland, nicknamed Blaufränkischland, has a red wine DAC for Blaufränkisch, while Weinviertel is the biggest region and holds half the country's Grüner Veltliner.
Wachau has its own three-level classification, all for dry wines: Steinfeder up to 11.5% alcohol, Federspiel from 11.5 to 12.5%, and Smaragd with a minimum of 12.5%.
Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd wines cannot be chaptalized or back-sweetened with süssreserve, and maximum residual sugar is 4 g/L for Federspiel and 9 g/L for Smaragd.
Smaragd grapes must reach at least 18.5°KMW, and the wines are not released before May 1 after harvest; good examples can age for more than 20 years.
Vinea Wachau, founded in 1983, has more than 200 members who own more than 85% of the vineyard land, and it created the classification still used today.
Vineyards are terraced into steep, rocky Danube banks, with rock outcrops and loess soils and gneiss, granite and slate higher up.
Riesling is often planted on the steep gneiss hillsides near the river, while Grüner Veltliner, the most widely planted grape, thrives on the loess and sand of the lower banks.
The Niagara Peninsula is Canada's largest wine-producing region, covering 13,600 acres.
It is bounded by Lake Ontario to the north, the Niagara River to the east, the Welland River to the south and Hamilton to the west.
The Niagara Escarpment rises 581 feet above sea level and provides slopes and elevations, and soils vary so much that VQA recognizes 10 sub-appellations here.
Ontario is the world's largest producer of ice wine, and as of 2019 it makes approximately 90 per cent of Canada's ice wine.
Lake Ontario moderates air temperature, and the main grapes are Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot noir and Cabernet Franc.
Casablanca Valley is in Valparaíso region, stretches roughly 19 miles east to west.
It quickly became known for white wines, notably Sauvignon blanc and Chardonnay, and for Pinot noir, which thrives in the cooler climate.
Free-draining clay and sandy soils encourage nematodes, so grafting onto nematode-resistant rootstocks is common, unlike the rest of Chile, where vines are mostly ungrafted.
Casablanca is the main exception to Chile's reliable weather, with more vintage variation because it sits close to the Pacific.
It divides into three sub-regions: Alto Maipo, Central Maipo and Pacific Maipo.
Alto Maipo lies in the Andes foothills, where cold nights, hot days and poor, porous, rocky soil stress the vines and give bold, elegant Cabernet Sauvignon.
Central Maipo is the warmest and driest part, with rocky alluvial soils and drip irrigation, and Cabernet Sauvignon dominates alongside some Carmenere.
Pacific Maipo has coastal influence and alluvial soils, and is a popular place to experiment with white grapes, most notably Sauvignon blanc.
Soils show high salinity from Maipo river irrigation and low potassium, and the valley sits directly across the Andes from Mendoza Province.
